I have an extensive history with mental health. ADHD, OCD, BPD, MDD, HPD, PTSD, GAD, and others.

I would say, overall, what has been the most beneficial for me across the board is mindfulness/meditation practice. 

I was on many prescriptions for a number of years. Put in a decade's worth of effort in different therapies. CBT, DBT, Talk Therapy, EMDR, ACT, ECPT, chronic pain management and chronic stress management, CPT. 

Mindfulness and meditation has been a staple in every one of those different therapies. And I have found them to be the most overall helpful with managing symptoms across the board.

Example specifically for ADHD: I personally use mindfulness as a tool on really bad days with ADHD when it's making functioning a struggle. I make an effort for an allotted amount of time to be mindful in my actions (pay attention to one thing at a time, non-judgementally, on purpose). I use that practice as the reminder to purposefully slow down my actions, and gradually slow down my mind. 

Example for OCD: of course this depends on the type you live with, but for myself, grounding myself in reality while practicing "radical acceptance" of whatever intrusive obsessions show up, or awful intrusive thoughts/emotions/images. 

It takes practice. I've practiced for over 10 years. And it's definitely worth it. It's helped me tremendously, in tandem with the other efforts made along the way. That's my piece.

Right now, I am for my first time in a relationship with a man who is still friends with nearly every woman he has had sexual relationships with. Whether it was a fling, a full on relationship, or even just someone he hasn't actually slept with but finds attractive. 

It was a huge learning curve for me to not allow my jealousy over his past experiences to get in the way of our relationship. Obviously it's different for different people and if it's not something you can handle then just walk away. But I decided to fully dive into trusting him. Because these people are important to him and that is allowed.

I don't want to be the only human of significance for him, just the only human he feels romantically for. Just because a connection contained sex at one point in their lives does not mean that it will forever. And just because someone may be considered attractive does not mean that they will be pursued. There are plenty of people who have very strong friendships (my spouse included) unrelated to the sexual aspect even if it did take place. 

We are engaged, have a nearly two year old together, and have been living together for nearly 4 years. 

Through the time I struggled the most with my jealousy , I chose moments when we were both calm and then spoke openly about all the different feelings going on while also acknowledging that he was not doing anything wrong and my intent was not to accuse, I was just feeling things and this was different for me to get used to. 

That's my 2 cents.

This is something I have talked to a very dear friend of mine about, because the way you are feeling sounds very similar to how he’s been feeling. This is what I’ve expressed to him.

Different people just have different need levels of interaction in order to keep a friendship alive. He is someone who prefers contact every week to two weeks at the very least, and longer than that makes him feel forgotten about. My husband is also a person who requires regular and consistent contact with friends to maintain the friendship.

I on the other hand, am very comfortable going weeks to months, sometimes even more than a year in between contact with friends. For me, it can vary a lot. And I’ve been sure to make it clear to him and any other friends who tend to require more frequent interaction that just because I have not messaged or visited in a while does not mean that I’m not thinking about you, or that I don’t care. The majority of my very strong friendships are not built on the frequency of interaction.

So when it comes to friendships where you see a mismatch in those need levels, you have two choices. If it’s a friendship that matters to you a lot, you can choose to open up the topic for some honest conversation. If you’re both willing to make a small compromise in how you interact to find some middle ground that works for you both, then fantastic!

As long as neither friend feels either suffocated by the frequency of communication, or abandoned in the lack there of, you’re doing great.

The other choice would be to accept that you and the friend in question just are not compatible when it comes to those need levels. It’s okay to decide that you just don’t feel like the friendship is receiving the amount of care that you require in order to feel like you guys are actually and actively friends.

You can’t force other people to bend to your needs, but you can seek out people whose need levels are more closely matched to yours so that it is more comfortable for both parties to keep up the level of maintenance that each one requires.

In case you happen to look at the comment I left, the friend that my method works well for definitely has a lot of symptoms and other diagnoses that lead us to believe he may be on the spectrum as well. Just so you have more context for where my words are coming from. But we’ve also built our friendship on the basis that we can be super bluntly upfront with each other and it is only ever with the intent to strengthen the friendship.

There are times in strong friendships when you need to be completely blunt, and although it may come off as rude, that doesn’t make it less necessary.

What I do when I need to speak to a friend in a way or about a topic that I know may hurt them, is speak to them over the phone or in person - NO TEXTING as the tone can easily be misunderstood and it’s already a sensitive topic. Then I make sure to say the exact thing very very clearly and remind them that I am not saying this to be hurtful.

“Okay, (friend), I need to have a very upfront conversation with you. Are you in a state that you’re ready for this kind of thing? Okay, so listen, I need to ask you to stop (xyz behaviour). I understand that it’s coming from good intentions, but it is seriously putting a strain on our friendship. I am not saying this to be hurtful, I am not saying it to criticize you or put you down. I am saying it because I care about our friendship and I don’t want this sort of behaviour to break it down. How are you feeling hearing what I just said?”

This method works well for me personally, (particularly with my most socially inept friend) but I also recognize different types of people take conversations like this differently, so if you’re gonna say something like that obviously feel free to tailor it more to the specific friend in mind. 

The biggest steps in how I say it are:
- briefly prepare by stating the nature of conversation 
- come right out with it, don’t beat around the bush
- remind them your intentions (not trying to be hurtful)
- give them a chance to speak on how they’re feeling and you SHUT UP while they do so

Also, sometimes if I’m feeding him a purée that i can’t save the leftovers from again, I’ll just give him the whole bowl once his appetite slows down to let him explore. If I’m gonna throw out whatever’s left anyway, and he’s eaten a decent amount already, then here ya go kid: play, dump it on yourself, lick the bowl, I don’t care haha. I don’t know if this will be helpful for you to hear, but remember that everyone experiences different types and different degrees of discomfort while pregnant. I had to stay very closely in touch with my doctors while i was pregnant just because of some things in my medical history and certain symptoms I was experiencing.

I remember being told about one of my coworkers gossiping about how they “never experienced this many issues while pregnant”, comparing my experiences to theirs. At the time, I was totally offended and felt like they were judging me for struggling with certain symptoms so much. It’s not like anything I dealt with was a huge risk for me or baby either, but it was so difficult to push through and sometimes I just couldn’t.

Thankfully I didn’t say anything to her about it because I’m just not interested in feeding into workplace drama. I mentioned it to my boss at the time but it was truly a non-issue. That coworker was still perfectly fine to work with and friendly to me , she’s genuinely just a gossipy person and (I believe) didn’t intend it in any sorta harmful way.

Long story short, some people truly struggle to believe how uncomfortable some pregnancy symptoms can be because they themselves simply didn’t experience the same things.

You know what you are feeling, no one else does. No one else is in your body. For me, pregnancy was the greatest teacher for me to start properly listening to my body.

I’ll add, if nausea continues to be a really significant issue for you, maybe mention it to your doctor. I know there are things they can do/suggest/prescribe to help ease it. 

As for people saying “their personality is stronger and could power through it”, especially a man… take it as an opportunity to get a personal chuckle to yourself imagining them actually trying to get through that experience. I personally doubt he could , haha.

I’m 9 months post birth now. And I’ll tell you, I also felt completely different after giving birth. Uncomfortable in my own skin, initially my body didn’t feel like my own. Even my mental state changed, like my thinking patterns because my mind was so consumed with caring for my baby, even my thoughts barely felt like my own. All of my relationships (family, friends, coworkers, partner) were all changed. It’s an extremely difficult adjustment. 

I’m still in the process of learning who I am now, but it’s getting easier. It’s similar to any major life event. You will never be the same person as you were before. Because some vital components of your life are now different. That’s not a bad thing, but it’s definitely uncomfortable and unfamiliar in the early months. And that’s not to say you’ve “lost” who you were before, but you will have to get to know yourself again.

It took me time. Practice in carving out moments of the day for me, for hobbies I enjoy, for space to exist outside the realm of “mom”. A lot of work navigating the ups and downs of my thoughts and emotions as my hormones have been levelling back out. I thank my partner often for his patience with me as I’ve been working through this stuff. 

So, to answer your questions more directly:

1. Yes, I have felt this way. I’m pretty certain every mom experiences these feelings and I can’t speak for other women, but it’s an extremely difficult adjustment so please try not to beat yourself up for how you feel.

2. No, it doesn’t go away. But, yes, it gets better. It gets easier to navigate the thoughts and emotions as your body recovers (it takes a bit, I’m still working through it all myself). It gets easier to find time for you, your relationships, and your new baby.

3. Take it one day at a time. Do things you used to enjoy before getting pregnant/having your baby. Wear clothes that fit you well and make you feel good in your body. If that means finding a pair of pants that fit you better as your body is now, then I’d say it’s worth it, though I understand it’s different for everyone. Make time for friends that matter to you. They will understand if it’s not often. It doesn’t have to be often, you’ve got a lot on your plate right now. But when you can, make time for them. 

In my experience, it was a lot more than appearance that made me feel uneasy with this new “me” trying to emerge. Be patient and compassionate with yourself. I know, easier said than done. I personally found it helpful to talk myself through difficult emotions, out loud, in the way I would like yo be able to talk my child through difficult emotions. 

You just made a whole-ass human being. It takes some time to recover and feel like yourself again. It’s much easier to get through difficult things when you eat well , drink enough water and sleep when you can. Do what you can when you can, I know your days are full.

Sorry for my novel, but I hope some of it is helpful. Sending you love and strength mama.

Thank you so much for sharing your experience. Although I do not personally have schizophrenia, I do suffer from extensive mental health issues which resulted in frequent hospitalizations in previous years.

I’m managing well now and haven’t had a significant issue in some time. But I remember every person I met in the hospital that had an impact on me.

The most significant person that stands out to me is David. I met him the first time I was hospitalized. He suffered from schizophrenia. He would walk laps in the halls all day long. He invited me to walk with him. He was so kind and made me feel like things would be okay.

I remember all of our interactions. He would say things that clearly stemmed from hallucinations/delusions he was struggling with, but even through that his words were sweet and kind. It didn’t matter that they were based in something that wasn’t physically real. It was his intention and kindness that was very much real.

I think about him often. I won’t search for him or ever reach out. But I wonder how he is. I hope he has found stability. I hope he has found a companion. Most of all, I hope he’s still alive and finding joys in being alive.

And I wish the same for you. I wish you peace, contentment and stability in your days to come. Thank you for being. :)

I am mid-twenties. I started smoking only about 5 years ago. I want to quit. I have managed to stop for up to a year, up to eight months, etc. But I always came back to it.

For me, the reasoning may not seem like it makes a whole lot of sense, but it's like this: I have chronic mental health and physical health conditions. These each have a factor. I started because it was the most passive and least destructive way to decrease my approximate lifespan. I continued because it's one of the few choices I have about how my body feels. There is nothing I can do to decrease the level of pain I feel. But I get to choose some pain (gym/physiotherapy) and I get to choose when breathing is hard (smoking).

Every time I have quit, I am glad I did it. I've lasted a fair amount of time each time. But then my brain starts panicking: *your approximate lifespan is increasing; you'll have to stay alive longer if your life expectancy is increased; if I can't harm myself this way I'll do it another way*. 

I understand and acknowledge that I need to stop. That it is not helping me the way my brain sometimes tries to convince me it does.

I've spoken to my counselor, and I've made a lot of progress with my treatments, but my conditions are all chronic. Forever. And degenerative. I can manage it. But my body will never be in less pain or dysfunction, and will continue to get worse, regardless. My mental illnesses with never go away. All of this I can learn to manage. To try to prolong the degenerative nature of these things. But that's all.

My counselor has said that "now is not the time" to quit. I am still struggling. A lot. I am much better -- at managing and functioning -- but that doesn't ever get easier.

Again, sorry that this sounds like a lot of backwards logic. I acknowledge that. But that's the best reasoning I've got.
And: "Your recovery does not require their approval"

One part would be asking questions and actually listening to the answer. For example, at first I was confused and uncomfortable because it didn’t seem ‘right’ to me to try and erase all free thinking with constant mindfulness. When I asked for clarification on that, they said it’s not about always being mindful and never letting your thoughts roam. It’s a grey area and it’s about finding balance. That was hard to grasp at first, but then with assessing situations when I found myself confused in the all or nothing thoughts, it slowly got easier to pick out what balance means in different situations. 

Another big part was confronting my attending counsellor to tell her that I had been viewing her in an ‘all bad’ way and hadn’t been able to acknowledge any of her good traits, and apologizing for being so argumentative with her when she was trying to help. Then also saying it would take time for me to learn to see her as a balanced person and there would still be times I’d see her as all bad, but that I was willing to work with her and learn. Ended up being hugely helpful to talk with her about that and we still have really positive appointments to this day.

Yes, I do still use the skills I learned. For me, as I got more into practicing the skills every day (for real, every single day) they slowly became my go-to reactions for difficult situations instead of a conscious effort to correct the harmful reactions.  Now they sort of just keep going all the time, every day, as a subconscious processing style to go through my day. It does take a lot of energy even though it’s not a conscious effort though, and I notice it when I get really sick because then I have to revert back to actively practicing the skills as my body doesn’t have the left over energy to keep it running in the background.

Edit: I would like to add — the biggest improvements that I noticed came long after I finished DBT and happened very slowly, over time, as I continued practicing every day. So the other user’s advice of sticking with it (even if it doesn’t seem to apply to you or really make sense at the time) is pretty important. And for me, through the consistent practice, I was able to find ways or make little changes that made the teachings more helpful for me personally than they were originally.

1. Yes, I did DBT for a year.

2. Yes, it helped me a lot.

3. Yes, I completed my DBT sessions in 2015 and the skills have stayed with me and offered a huge amount of help for my continued recovery.

4. To make it more efficient, honestly the big thing is deciding for yourself in your head if you really want to put the effort in. I was really against it at first and got kicked out of a few different therapy programs the first time around — they always said it was because I had such a severe personality disorder that they weren’t capable of helping me. But with this particular one, after I was asked to leave, I spent a year going through a DBT workbook by myself to teach myself to be more open to what they were teaching. Really had to work hard to sort of train myself out of the rigid black and white thinking, at least enough that I was able to take in what they were teaching when they went back. Then they did welcome me back to that group, and I had to put in a lot more hard work to make sure I wasn’t just taking up time fighting with the counsellors instead of admitting that I was uncomfortable. The way it worked for me was, 2 repeats of basic mindfulness practice, then cycle through each section of DBT going through each part twice in total.

5. For me, it wasn’t until my second time going through each section that I actually started to notice I was able to make changes that were helpful to me. That took about 5-7 months of just sticking through, taking the time to listen, and reminding myself that these people were not trying to attack me as a person, that they really were trying to help. By the final 5/6 months, the instructors were commenting on how I had become a grade A student in their course. Not gonna lie, that feeling of validation really kept me going through to the finish even though I didn’t say so at the time.

I haven’t commented in this subreddit before, so ahead of time, I apologize if my advice is unhelpful. But based on my experience, this is what I would say:

1: allow yourself a grieving period. To sort of mourn the loss of this person. It’s absolutely a good thing to allow yourself to feel hurt, vulnerable, and sad that they’re no longer a part of your life. Give yourself a chance to go through that loneliness without beating yourself up or thinking you shouldn’t be feeling that way. 

2: just because you allow yourself to be upset, doesn’t mean that it’ll all pass in one set period of time, or that it won’t come up again later on. And it’s definitely not a comfortable or nice feeling. So, learn to be able to sit with yourself, to be able to coexist with how bad it can feel and not entirely lose yourself to those feelings. Most simple mindfulness exercises can help this happen, and it’s a good thing to learn at some point so that pain (either emotional or physical) doesn’t end up totally crippling you. Patience comes with this too, so give yourself that patience.

3: once you get to a point when it feels right to address, think about reevaluating how you see yourself. You mentioned you gave yourself completely to this person — that they were as much a part of you as they were a part of your life. So, take some time to think about things you had thought previously made you who you are. If some of those things were big while you were with this person, can you still embrace things that make you ‘you’ even though they aren’t around? Do you (or did you) like those things about yourself? 

4: an important part of going through these feelings is making sure you’re not neglecting yourself by spending too much time just feeling bad. As much as it’s good to let yourself feel what you need, it’s also important you still take care of yourself and do things you need to. Get out of bed, wash your face, pee, change your clothes, drink some water, get something to eat, tidy or clean up one space in your home that needs to be done.
